title: Trump Removes Rex Tillerson and Nominates Mike Pompeo as Secretary of State
description_short: Trump fired Rex Tillerson as Secretary of State and nominated Mike Pompeo to replace him.
description_medium: On March 13, 2018, President Donald Trump announced Rex Tillerson’s removal as secretary of state and chose CIA Director Mike Pompeo to replace him, subject to Senate confirmation. Trump cited disagreements with Tillerson, particularly over the Iran nuclear agreement. The announcement followed months of friction and came as the administration prepared for possible talks with North Korea.
description_long:
President Donald Trump announced on March 13, 2018, that he was removing Secretary of State Rex Tillerson and choosing CIA Director Mike Pompeo to succeed him. The change followed months of friction between Trump and his top diplomat, including disagreements over Iran, North Korea and other foreign-policy issues. Trump publicly identified the Iran nuclear agreement as a point of disagreement and described Pompeo as sharing his approach.

The timing placed a transition at the State Department alongside preparations for a possible presidential meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. White House officials said Trump wanted the new team in place before a summit. Tillerson said he would delegate his responsibilities to Deputy Secretary John Sullivan that evening, while his tenure would formally end on March 31. Pompeo’s appointment remained subject to Senate confirmation. The announcement therefore removed the incumbent diplomatic leader while leaving the proposed successor awaiting the required Senate process.

title: Trump Announces Michael Atkinson’s Removal and Places Him on Administrative Leave
description_short: Trump notified Congress on April 3, 2020, that he intended to remove Michael Atkinson and immediately placed the intelligence inspector general on leave.
description_medium: On April 3, 2020, Trump notified Congress that he intended to remove Intelligence Community Inspector General Michael Atkinson, citing lost confidence. Atkinson immediately went on administrative leave pending removal after the thirty-day notice period. He had handled the Ukraine whistleblower complaint. Bipartisan senators questioned the leave and demanded a fuller explanation, saying a bare statement of lost confidence did not satisfy the statutory safeguard.
description_long: On April 3, 2020, President Donald Trump placed Intelligence Community Inspector General Michael Atkinson on administrative leave for thirty days pending his removal. Trump’s notification to Congress cited a loss of confidence in Atkinson. A bipartisan group of senators objected that this explanation lacked the details Congress expected under the inspector general removal safeguards. They also questioned whether immediately sidelining Atkinson undermined the required advance notice and Congress’s opportunity to discuss the decision. Atkinson had handled the Ukraine whistleblower complaint that figured in Trump’s first impeachment. After determining that the complaint involved an urgent concern, he forwarded it to the director of national intelligence. When Atkinson and acting Director Joseph Maguire disagreed about sending it to Congress, Atkinson notified lawmakers of that disagreement. Maguire ultimately transmitted the complaint itself. The distinction matters: Atkinson’s role was to assess and report the concern through the oversight process, rather than independently deliver the complaint to Congress. The removal raised questions about watchdog independence, while the senators’ objections constituted oversight criticism rather than a judicial determination that Trump’s action was unlawful.

title: Trump Removes State Department Inspector General Steve Linick
description_short: Trump removed State Department IG Steve Linick in May 2020 amid inquiries involving Mike Pompeo; motive remains disputed.
description_medium: Trump removed State Department Inspector General Steve Linick on May 15, 2020, amid inquiries involving Secretary Mike Pompeo. Congressional committees said Linick confirmed investigations into alleged misuse of government resources and Pompeo’s emergency arms-sale declaration. Pompeo denied knowing about the resource inquiry. Lawmakers investigated possible retaliation, while Linick disputed the administration’s explanations for removing him.
description_long: President Donald Trump removed State Department Inspector General Steve Linick on May 15, 2020. The following day, Senator Bob Menendez and Representative Eliot Engel announced an investigation into the firing and requested that the White House and State Department preserve relevant records. They also sought information about Stephen Akard, whom the department had announced would lead its inspector general office. The lawmakers alleged that the removal could be retaliation for scrutiny of Secretary of State Mike Pompeo. After a June 3 interview, congressional committees reported that Linick confirmed two pending matters involving Pompeo: alleged misuse of government resources by the secretary and his wife, and the secretary’s emergency declaration used for weapons sales. According to that account, Linick said senior department officials knew about the investigations. Pompeo had denied knowing about the resource inquiry on May 18. The committees also reported that Linick rejected the administration’s explanations for his removal as misplaced or unfounded. These accounts establish a dismissal during active oversight and a dispute about its justification. They do not resolve the allegation of retaliation or establish that the underlying inquiries proved wrongdoing.

title: Trump Grants a Full Pardon to Otis Gordon
description_short: The archived White House says Trump granted a full pardon to Otis Gordon on December 22, 2020.
description_medium: President Donald Trump granted a full pardon to Otis Gordon on December 22, 2020. The White House described Gordon as a pastor at Life Changer’s International Ministries who mentored at-risk young people after a drug conviction. Senator Tim Scott supported the pardon. The Justice Department lists Gordon’s case in the District of South Carolina among the pardons granted that day.
description_long:
President Donald Trump granted a full pardon to Otis Gordon on December 22, 2020. The Justice Department lists the pardon under that date and identifies Gordon’s federal case in the District of South Carolina. Its entry describes the offense as selling, distributing, or dispensing a controlled substance. It records a January 11, 1993 sentence of 85 or 86 months in prison, as amended, followed by 48 months of supervised release. The listing leaves that one-month distinction unresolved.

The White House announcement described Gordon’s conviction as possession with intent to distribute. It said he subsequently became a pastor at Life Changer’s International Ministries and mentored at-risk youths in his community. The announcement also noted that Gordon led a prayer session at the United States Capitol in 2015 following the shooting at a Bible study in Charleston, South Carolina. Senator Tim Scott supported the pardon and praised Gordon’s work helping young men avoid the difficulties he had faced. The action granted a full pardon; it was not announced as a reduction of an ongoing prison sentence.

title: Pardons Steven Benjamin Floyd
description_short: Trump granted a presidential pardon to Steven Benjamin Floyd as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: Donald Trump pardoned Steven Benjamin Floyd on January 19, 2021, for a bank-robbery-by-extortion conviction. Floyd received a 30-month sentence in 2008. The White House identified Representative Mark Green as a supporter and cited Floyd’s military service and community work. It said Floyd had been released in 2009 and subsequently raised a family and operated a car repair business.
description_long: Donald Trump granted Steven Benjamin Floyd a full pardon on January 19, 2021. Floyd had pleaded guilty to one count of bank robbery by extortion. The Justice Department lists his Southern District of Mississippi sentence, imposed January 3, 2008, as 30 months, with the final six months to be served in a halfway house, three years of supervised release, and a $2,500 fine. The White House’s announcement identified Representative Mark Green as a supporter of the pardon. It described Floyd as a Marine who enlisted at 17 and earned a combat action ribbon in Iraq. According to that announcement, Floyd left prison in 2009, later raised a family, and operated a successful car repair business. The administration also cited his assistance in extinguishing fires during unrest and his free car repairs for widows and disabled veterans. Trump thanked him for military service and community involvement. Those were the administration’s stated considerations for granting clemency after his prison term had ended.

title: Trump Granted William E. Henry a Full Pardon on January 19, 2021
description_short: Trump granted William E. “Ed” Henry a full and unconditional pardon for his federal theft-of-government-property conviction on January 19, 2021.
description_medium: Donald Trump granted William E. “Ed” Henry a full and unconditional pardon on January 19, 2021. Henry had pleaded guilty to theft of government property arising from assistance in obtaining improper Medicare reimbursements. He received two years’ probation and a $4,000 fine in May 2019. The White House identified Senator Tommy Tuberville as supporting the pardon.
description_long: On January 19, 2021, President Donald Trump granted William E. Henry, also known as Ed Henry, a full and unconditional pardon. Henry’s conviction concerned assistance in obtaining Medicare reimbursements to which physicians were not entitled. According to federal prosecutors’ account of court documents, Henry owned MyPractice24 and served for part of the relevant period as its chief executive. The company provided chronic care management services under contracts with doctors, who billed Medicare and paid the company a share of the reimbursements. Prosecutors said Henry arranged kickbacks for a physician and staff in return for patient referrals and helped the physician reward patients by waiving required copayments. Henry pleaded guilty to one theft-of-government-property count in January 2019. On May 2, 2019, he was sentenced to two years’ probation and a $4,000 fine. The pardon instrument identifies the Middle District of Alabama conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 641 and also lists a $100 special assessment. The White House identified Senator Tommy Tuberville as a supporter of the pardon.

title: Trump Commuted Mark Shapiro’s 85-Year Prison Sentence to Time Served
description_short: A December 2020 clemency warrant commuted Mark Shapiro’s prison sentence to time served; DOJ lists the fraud convictions and restitution.
description_medium: On December 23, 2020, Trump commuted Mark Shapiro’s prison sentence to time served. The DOJ clemency instrument records an 85-year sentence, three years of supervised release, and $22,075,631 restitution for securities, wire, and mail fraud offenses. The White House cited sentence disparity against plea offers, time served, and support from advocates and victims as its rationale. Those reasons are the administration’s account, not an independent finding that the sentence was unjust.
description_long: On December 23, 2020, Donald Trump commuted Mark Shapiro’s 85-year prison sentence to time served. Shapiro had been convicted in the Southern District of New York of conspiracy to commit securities, wire and mail fraud, securities fraud, wire fraud and mail fraud. The October 21, 2010 sentence also included three years of supervised release and $22,075,631 in restitution. The commutation left the unpaid restitution balance, a $500 special assessment, supervised release and other sentence components intact. Federal prosecutors described the Cobalt real estate investment scheme as involving false claims about the companies’ history and property holdings, and concealment of Shapiro’s and Irving Stitsky’s control and prior convictions. The White House argued that Shapiro’s prison sentence was disproportionate to a five-to-seven-year plea offer and said he had served longer than that offer. It cited rehabilitation and support from advocates and some victims. These were the administration’s stated grounds for clemency, rather than a court ruling overturning the fraud convictions.

title: Trump commutes James Brian Cruz’s prison sentence to time served
description_short: Trump commuted James Brian Cruz’s prison sentence to time served on January 19, 2021, retaining five years of supervised release and unpaid financial obligations.
description_medium: On January 19, 2021, Donald Trump commuted James Brian Cruz’s prison sentence to time served. Cruz had received 480 months for methamphetamine conspiracy in 2001. The warrant retained five years of supervised release and unpaid financial obligations. The White House cited his work and mentoring in prison and identified supporters including Alice Johnson and Dallas pastor Robert Jeffress.
description_long: Donald Trump commuted James Brian Cruz’s prison sentence to time served on January 19, 2021. Cruz had been convicted in the Western District of Texas of conspiracy to possess more than 500 grams of methamphetamine with intent to distribute. His June 26, 2001 sentence included 480 months in prison, five years of supervised release and a $25,000 fine. The commutation warrant records that he had been in federal custody since June 29, 2000, and was incarcerated at the federal prison in Seagoville, Texas. It identifies April 10, 2034 as his projected release date before clemency. Trump’s grant reduced the prison term while leaving the five-year supervision term, its conditions, unpaid fine balance, $100 special assessment and other sentence components in effect. In announcing clemency, the White House cited Cruz’s work and mentoring of other prisoners. It identified Alice Johnson, pastor Robert Jeffress and lawyer Kelly Shackelford among his supporters. The administration presented those rehabilitation claims as reasons to give him another chance.
